nuggets.title: Centralized Redis Outage Causes Total API Blackout

scenario.symptoms: API Gateway endpoints return 500 Internal Server Errors across all routes. Upstream services report 0 incoming requests while overall API availability drops to zero.
scenario.interviewerSetup: The primary Redis cluster hosting rate limit counters experienced a network split and stopped responding to queries. Because the API Gateway was configured to fail closed on counter lookup failures, all incoming client traffic is dropped.

incident.headline: Redis cluster outage causes API Gateway to fail closed, dropping 100% of legitimate customer traffic.

agenda.goal: Implement fail-open behavior coupled with local gateway fallback counters to ensure high API availability during store outages.
agenda.opener: Our central Redis counter store is unreachable and the gateway is blocking all incoming traffic. How do you restore traffic immediately and structurally solve this failure mode?

evidence.strong: Proposes toggling the gateway to fail-open with short connect timeouts, while implementing an in-memory local fallback counter (e.g. Guava/Caffeine cache) on each gateway instance to prevent backend DB overload.
evidence.adequate: Suggests changing gateway configuration to fail-open so traffic passes through, but misses adding local fallback rate limiting to protect backend databases.
evidence.weak: Suggests restarting Redis or adding more nodes without addressing the fail-closed code logic in the gateway.

misconceptions.pattern: Believing failing closed is safer because it protects the backend at all costs.
misconceptions.challenge: If failing closed turns a localized Redis outage into a total API blackout for 100% of users, is that acceptable for business availability SLAs?

probes: How do you protect backend services from being flooded when failing open during an attack?
What connect and read timeouts should the gateway enforce when querying Redis?
hints: Consider what is worse: serving slightly un-ratelimited requests or rejecting all valid customers.
Can the gateway maintain an approximate counter locally in RAM when Redis does not respond in under 5ms?
agenda.referenceFix: Configure gateway to fail-open on Redis timeout (>5ms threshold). Fall back to in-memory local token buckets per gateway instance during Redis failure to enforce soft limits and shield backend DBs.

nuggets.title: Hot API Key Saturates Single Redis Shard

scenario.symptoms: Latency spikes to 1,500ms for high-tier API users. CPU usage on a single Redis cluster shard hits 100%, while adjacent shards remain under 5% utilization.
scenario.interviewerSetup: A large enterprise client started a massive data ingestion job sending 60,000 requests per second. All requests for this client's API key hash to Shard 3 of the Redis cluster, creating an execution bottleneck.

incident.headline: Single hot API key concentrates traffic onto one Redis shard, creating single-thread CPU bottleneck.

agenda.goal: Mitigate hot key saturation using local gateway batching or split-key counter sharding.
agenda.opener: Adding more nodes to our Redis cluster didn't help because all requests for customer 'enterprise_123' hash to the same shard. How do you solve this hot-key bottleneck?

evidence.strong: Proposes either local memory batching (aggregating counts in gateway instances and syncing to Redis every 50-100ms) or sub-sharding hot keys (e.g., enterprise_123:shard_N) with periodic aggregation.
evidence.adequate: Suggests local in-memory caching of decision state on the gateway fleet, but lacks clear mechanism on how counter sync occurs across instances.
evidence.weak: Recommends expanding the Redis cluster size or adding read replicas, ignoring that Redis writes/eval scripts for a single key hit one primary node.

misconceptions.pattern: Assuming consistent hashing or cluster expansion resolves single-key bottlenecks.
misconceptions.challenge: If consistent hashing maps key 'enterprise_123' to Shard 3, will adding 10 more shards change where key 'enterprise_123' lands?

probes: If you aggregate local counts in gateway RAM before sending to Redis, how do you handle strict window limits?
How would key splitting (e.g. enterprise_123_sub1) change the execution pattern on Redis?
hints: Can individual API gateway instances batch counter updates locally for 50 milliseconds before writing to Redis?
What if a hot key's counter is split across N sub-keys distributed randomly across shards?
agenda.referenceFix: Implement local micro-batching on API Gateways: count requests in local memory for 50ms windows and issue atomic bulk INCRBY calls to Redis, reducing Redis ops by 90%+ for hot keys.

nuggets.title: Non-Atomic Counter Read-Write Allows Quota Bypass

scenario.symptoms: Audit logs show a client with a strict tier limit of 1,000 requests/minute successfully executed over 12,000 requests in a single second without receiving HTTP 429.
scenario.interviewerSetup: The gateway rate limiter code performs a GET for the user key, checks if key < limit in application code, and then issues INCR. Under extreme concurrency, hundreds of gateway threads read the old counter before any thread writes the increment.

incident.headline: Race condition in non-atomic GET-and-INCR check allows concurrent requests to bypass rate limits.

agenda.goal: Eliminate race conditions by executing counter read, increment, and expiration check atomically in Redis.
agenda.opener: Our logs show thousands of requests bypassing limits during concurrent bursts because gateway instances execute separate GET and INCR operations. How do you fix this data race?

evidence.strong: Replaces separate GET and write calls with atomic Redis Lua scripts or Redis EVALSHA commands executing atomic token bucket / window logic server-side.
evidence.adequate: Recommends using atomic Redis commands like INCRBY, but struggles to explain how window creation/TTL setting is executed atomically alongside increment.
evidence.weak: Suggests adding application-level locking (like Java synchronized locks) across distributed gateway instances.

misconceptions.pattern: Assuming separate Redis calls are atomic across distributed worker processes.
misconceptions.challenge: If 100 worker threads issue GET key at millisecond 0, what value do all 100 threads read before issuing INCR?

probes: How does a Lua script guarantee atomicity inside Redis?
What is the network footprint difference between executing 1 Lua script vs 3 round-trip Redis commands?
hints: Can we move the counter conditional check into Redis itself so network round-trips don't interleave?
How can Redis Lua scripts run complex token bucket calculations atomically?
agenda.referenceFix: Refactor rate limit evaluation into an atomic Redis Lua script that checks capacity, updates timestamp/tokens, and returns a binary allowed/rejected flag in a single atomic execution.
